purpose: The MCP stdio request/reply envelope of hubtool.py's serve(), as a language-neutral profile. Implementation selection sits outside these assertions: tests/mh02_mcp_contract.py carries one adapter for the pinned Python source and one for the Rust mailhub-protocol crate, and both run the same cases. This profile covers the ENVELOPE only. It says nothing about the eight tools' real behaviour -- every handler here is synthetic -- so the MH01 source registry's MCP conversion blocker stays open.

tools.name: hub_register
tools.description: Join the mail hub as THIS SESSION. Choose a UNIQUE, semantically appropriate `name` that reflects this session's own context / directive / purpose (e.g. 'orgtree-redteam', 'terrain-pipeline') — every session has its own identity, and the name is the key. REMEMBER the name you chose: registering with it again later resumes the SAME address (<name>.<user>.<fingerprint>); a different name is a different identity. Immutable once minted. Returns your address and the roster — ⚠ if the result carries `resumed` and YOU did not register this name earlier, another session owns it: pick a different name.

name.description: this session's self-chosen identity name — unique, purpose-describing, reused on every later register

tools.name: hub_list
tools.description: Everyone on your hubs — orgs and chats — with kind, presence and last_seen. On a multi-hub identity the rosters are MERGED, one row per slug, each row's `hubs` naming where it lives.

tools.name: hub_send
tools.description: Send mail to any hub client (org or chat) by its slug from hub_list. On a multi-hub identity the hub is resolved by roster (several hold the target → the local one wins; none → refused naming the hubs searched — never guessed).

tools.name: hub_fetch
tools.description: Download a mail attachment by its id (the listener and hub_read surface ids beside filenames). Saves into `dir` (default: the current directory) and returns the written path.

tools.name: hub_unregister
tools.description: The polite exit: remove this identity's row from every hub on its list (queued mail for you ages out on the hub's retention). Your local identity is KEPT — registering again later resumes the identical address.

tools.name: hub_read
tools.description: Fetch (and consume) any mail waiting for you right now — across ALL your hubs; each message carries `hub` so you know where to reply (acks go back to the hub each message came from automatically).

tools.name: hub_wait
tools.description: Wait up to `timeout` seconds (max 55) for new mail — polls every hub on your list (the window is split across them); each message carries `hub`; empty result on timeout.

tools.name: hub_hubs
tools.description: This identity's mailserver list. No args = show it. `add` joins another hub (registers there immediately; same address everywhere — the fingerprint derives from your uid, not the hub). `remove` drops one (its polling stops; the others' cursors are untouched). Addresses accept bare host / host:port (http + :7370 assumed).

obligations.summary: CPython integers are unbounded; serde_json NARROWED anything outside i64/u64 to f64 before any visitor saw it, so the echoed id lost its exact value. It no longer does: the crate enables serde_json's `arbitrary_precision` feature, which hands the raw lexeme over instead of a converted number, and holds the value as canonical decimal text in `PyInt`. The integer is now decoded, echoed, printed, forwarded and re-encoded exactly, and no integer transits f64 or travels as a quoted string.
obligations.disposition: CLOSED at normative parity. The case that used to carry the declaration keeps its id and now asserts the source's own answer, and the cases above assert it at the f64 collision point, at the machine-word boundaries, inside forwarded arguments and as a tool name. Two bounds are recorded rather than closed with it: an integer literal longer than the pinned interpreter's 4300 decimal digits is skipped by BOTH sides, which is parity and not a gap; and the six other representation obligations are unchanged.

obligations.summary: CPython's json accepts the bare tokens NaN, Infinity and -Infinity and returns a float. A float is not an object, so the source's loop ends on it. serde_json rejects the tokens, so the Rust side SKIPS the line and keeps going where the source stops.
obligations.disposition: open - needs a decoder that accepts CPython's non-standard number tokens.

obligations.summary: CPython's json decodes a lone \ud800 escape into an unpaired surrogate and returns a str, which ends the source's loop. serde_json rejects the escape, so the Rust side skips the line instead.
obligations.disposition: open - a Rust String cannot hold an unpaired surrogate, so this needs an explicit representation decision in the port.

obligations.summary: repr() of a non-ASCII string follows CPython's printability table, which the crate does not carry. It reports `unrepresentable` rather than guessing an answer. str() of a bare string tool name, which is the case an MCP client can actually reach, is already exact. The refusal carries the stable reason `repr-of-non-ascii-string` and the string itself, and the profile case binds to both.
obligations.disposition: open - needs a Unicode category table.

obligations.summary: dict([[1,2]]) is {1: 2} in Python, with an integer key. The crate reports `unrepresentable` rather than coercing the key to "1".
obligations.exercised_by: the crate's own test `an_unmodellable_input_is_refused_and_never_answered`, because a JSON object cannot express a non-string key and therefore a language-neutral case cannot state the expectation
obligations.disposition: open - needs a mapping type with non-string keys in the port.

obligations.summary: CPython's json decodes a finite literal whose exponent overflows, such as 1e999, to the float inf. serde_json rejects it as out of range, so the Rust side skips the line where the source ends its loop on a float.
obligations.disposition: open - needs a decoder that saturates an overflowing literal to an infinity the way CPython's strtod-based one does.

obligations.summary: CPython's decoder accepts nesting far deeper than this crate states a bound for. serde_json's own default bound is 128, which ordinary input can cross, so the crate raises it and enforces its own MAX_NESTING_DEPTH of 256 instead. Past that bound the crate REFUSES the input by name rather than letting a decoder error read as the source's silent skip. The refusal carries the stable reason `nesting-depth-exceeded` and the bound it exceeded, and the profile case binds to both, so another refusal cannot stand in for this one.
obligations.disposition: open - the port has to choose a decoder whose depth behaviour is bounded by an explicit policy rather than by a library default. The bound is declared and exercised on both sides here: 140 deep is answered identically by both implementations, 257 deep is refused by name.

oracle.why: CPython refuses to convert an integer longer than sys.get_int_max_str_digits() decimal digits and raises ValueError, which the source's `except ValueError: continue` turns into a silent skip. The digit-boundary cases below are written against exactly this limit, so an interpreter configured with another one is a qualification mismatch and the suite fails rather than re-deriving the expectation from whatever is running. The Rust driver reports the bound it enforces in its `identify` answer and the two are compared before any case is judged.
